newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole enter final day of campaigning.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole enter final day of campaigning.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole continued their frenzied last-minute campaigning on the final day before voters decide who will lead the country for the next four years.

Most polls showed Clinton with a shrinking but solid lead, while Republicans seemed increasingly likely to maintain control of both houses of Congress, potentially leaving Clinton with a clouded mandate for his second term.

Dole took a six-hour break from his unprecedented 96-hour around-the-clock campaign blitz on Sunday to nap and clean up, then continued his relentless attack on White House ethics and asked Ross Perot's supporters for their votes.
Addressing a rally of some 4,000 supporters in this city east of Los Angeles, Dole said Americans would show character mattered in the election.
"We are going to prevail because the American people have had enough," he said. "They've had enough and they're going to make a change."

Clinton, casting himself as the voice of centrist reason and sounding very presidential, appealed to voters to seek "common ground" and heal the racial, religious and cultural divisions tearing apart the country.

"We will never be what we ought to be if we allow our country to be led by those who believe we are better off on our own, and who seek to pursue that path by driving wedges between us and exploiting our fears and convincing us that our brothers and sisters of different races, different faiths, different walks of life, are our inherent enemies," he said.
"That is a prescription for disaster," he told St. Paul's African Episcopal Methodist Church in Tampa, Fla., where civil rights leader Martin Luther King once preached.

The Dole campaign, energised by poll data showing Clinton's edge narrowing after weeks of double-digit leads, continued hammering away at Clinton's ethics to woo undecided voters away from the Democrats.
The Reuters daily tracking poll showed Dole within four percentage points of Clinton. ABC had the president 11 points ahead and Gallup put the president's lead at 13 points.

Individual state polls gave Dole some reason for hope. He was running even with Clinton in Georgia and Tennessee, within five points in the key state of Ohio and led Clinton in Nevada -- all states Clinton carried in 1992.

Republicans also pulled ahead in the Reuters poll in the battle for Congress. The Republicans won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in 1994 for the first time in 40 years. This year, they have been targets of an all-out assault by Democrats and their labour union allies.
But two new polls released Sunday showed Dole's focus on the character issue has failed to change voters' minds.

The latest Harris Poll showed that by 45 percent to 39 percent voters tend to see Dole as more honest and trustworthy than Clinton, but two weeks ago, he had a wider lead of 44 percent to Clinton's 34 percent.

The poll of 1,029 likely voters conducted Nov. 1-3 also gave Clinton an overwhelming lead on most major policy issues, including education, the environment, jobs, health care and the economy. The margin of error was three percentage points.

A separate poll by the Pew Research Centre of 1,211 likely voters conducted Oct. 31 through Nov. 3, found Clinton leading Dole by 49 percent to 36 percent, with Perot grabbing eight percent and six percent undecided.
Potential damage from the campaign finance controversies dogging the Democrats in recent weeks appeared to be less than expected, the Pew pollsters said.

Fifty-six percent of the likely voters said they had closely followed news of improper campaign contributions to the Democratic National Committee, but only seven percent of Clinton backers said the charges raised serious doubts in their minds about voting for the president.
Additionally, the poll showed that Dole had the support of only 75 percent of those self-identifying as Republicans, compared to 85 percent of the Democrats supporting Clinton.
The sampling error was three percentage points.
